outcomes.absoluteFailure:
In the towns of Rhovanion, merchants' stories distinguish the great wolves of the mountains from those that accompany the Orcs. The former would be wild predators, while the latter would belong to a breed fashioned over generations for service in war. These animals, called Wargs, are said to have been raised in mountain caverns and accustomed from their youth to warriors' cries, the din of weapons, and the weight of riders. Their extraordinary size would result from patient breeding, the secrets of which the Orcs jealously guard. The largest serve as mounts for their chieftains, while smaller individuals are used to recover fugitives or guard paths leading to their lairs.

A tradition common in market towns claims that these beasts find structures built by Men difficult to endure. The scent of worked timber, tar, and the ironwork of bridges would recall the restraints of their training. They would hesitate to cross long causeways and footbridges suspended above water, whose vibrations disturb their balance. The inhabitants of riverside towns therefore believe that a well-guarded bridge affords protection against Wargs, even when a pack numbers many individuals on the opposite bank. The elders say that these great wolves always prefer to seek a natural ford rather than venture upon a human-built crossing, and that a caravan reaching a town's gates in time may cease to fear their pursuit.
outcomes.failure:
The inhabitants of northern towns know Wargs from the testimony of merchants, boatmen, and guards who watch the roads leading towards the mountains. These great wolves possess unusual strength and can travel considerable distances at speed. Convoys crossing wild country dread their ability to recover a trail, follow travellers for many hours, and move in groups whose members appear to understand one another. Some are powerful enough to carry an Orc warrior, and garrison accounts assign them an important role in scouting the roads used by merchants.

You also know the warnings passed down by caravan leaders concerning their howls. According to these tales, Orcs train their Wargs to employ different calls to signal a convoy's presence, the discovery of a passage, or the gathering of a force. Experienced travellers therefore learn to recognise certain cries, whose duration and number are said to reveal the proximity of Orc warriors. A succession of short howls would announce scattered scouts, while one prolonged call would indicate the gathering of a larger force. This practice would explain the remarkable coordination of Wargs, whose movements would depend upon a system of military signals perfected by their masters.
outcomes.partialSuccess:
In the towns of Rhovanion, Wargs are known as great malevolent wolves that frequent the mountains and wild regions, sometimes in the company of Orcs. Travellers' accounts ascribe to them a size greater than that of ordinary wolves, considerable endurance, and senses capable of recognising a trail long after its makers have passed. Some carry Orc warriors, while others accompany armed bands in pursuit of fugitives. Their speed and ability to move in packs make them dangerous to merchants travelling through country far from inhabited settlements.

You know that Wargs possess an intelligence exceeding that of wild animals. They exchange cries and howls whose meaning generally escapes Men. Their concerted movements may answer to common decisions even when no rider accompanies them. Road-wardens know their ability to recognise fords, narrow passages, and paths habitually used by travellers. The stories circulating in markets also stress that a pack may appear far from Orcish encampments and pursue an undertaking on its own account.
outcomes.success:
The trading communities of Rhovanion preserve detailed accounts of Wargs, gathered from travellers who journey along the roads between towns, mountains, and great forests. These testimonies describe creatures endowed with an intelligence of their own and capable of communicating in a language that belongs to them. Wargs can exchange warnings, acknowledge their leaders' decisions, and organise common enterprises. Their alliance with the Orcs rests on shared interests, yet their packs retain their autonomy. Some individuals serve as mounts, while others accompany armed bands as scouts or pursuers. The most reliable accounts also describe gatherings of Wargs that act independently of any Orcish force.

Merchants and guards acquainted with these creatures attach great importance to the routes they frequent. A Warg can recognise a caravan's habitual movements, follow a trail to a ford, and seek another passage when a road becomes unfavourable. Several individuals may separate to take different paths, then rejoin one another through the calls they exchange. Bridges, causeways, and fortified structures constitute obstacles according to their disposition and defence, but Wargs are capable of understanding their use and crossing them when circumstances permit. Their knowledge of the terrain, combined with their speed, enables them to pursue travellers attempting to change their route.

The traditions of the northern towns also distinguish information gathered by soldiers from that brought by caravans. The former chiefly know the employment of Wargs in Orcish enterprises; the latter report their appearances on roads, their movements, and the consequences of their attacks. Comparing these testimonies makes it possible to recognise behaviour common to several packs. Men possessing such experience understand that Wargs are an independent threat, capable of exploiting the movements of travellers as readily as the warlike enterprises of their allies.
outcomes.absoluteSuccess:
The deepest knowledge of the urbanised Northmen combines memories of ancient conflicts, testimony handed down by merchants, and traditions preserved among neighbouring peoples. It distinguishes Wargs from natural wolves by their intelligence, language, and ability to form common designs. Wargs possess their own leaders, gather to deliberate, and can prepare attacks before they have even met their Orcish allies. Their association with the latter rests on shared interests and common hostility towards the Free Peoples. A pack may nevertheless pursue aims different from those of an Orc-band, abandon an enterprise that has become unfavourable, or begin a hunt without receiving orders from outside.

The memory of towns and market settlements makes it possible to understand their movements on a broader scale than any isolated encounter. Information collected in several settlements may reveal a pack following trade routes, exploiting frequented passages, or accompanying the movements of armed groups. Wargs recognise the routes that slow convoys and can coordinate their approaches along several paths. Their howls are communications whose meaning depends upon their own language, and their number seldom provides, by itself, a reliable indication of the Orcish forces present in a region. Experienced guards distinguish direct observations from the interpretations travellers place upon the sounds heard during the night.

The oldest traditions speak of an origin linked to the corruption of wolves by the powers of the Shadow. Other accounts, carried by Elves or peoples who preserve the memory of the Elder Days, distinguish Wargs from the Werewolves that served Morgoth. This distinction remains important to learned Men, for beings of different natures can present similar appearances. Wargs belong to the wolf-like creatures whose malice is accompanied by organised intelligence; tales of their supernatural origin explain their place among the servants of the Shadow, while travellers' testimony makes it possible to recognise their observable habits and abilities.

gmNote: GM verification: absolute failure — imaginary aversion to bridges and human-built structures; failure — erroneous interpretation of the howls as a military code imposed by Orcs; successful results — independent language, commercial memory, and concerted movements.
